steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Dramatic irony: audience knows something characters don't — creates tension, humour or foreboding.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Soliloquy: character alone on stage speaking thoughts — reveals inner truth to audience.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Aside: character briefly shares thoughts with audience — conspiratorial, breaks fourth wall.

steps.title: Key Fact
steps.body: Cross-cutting: switching between two scenes — creates contrast, parallel or tension.

steps.title: Try it yourself
steps.body: Describe three dramatic devices a playwright might use to reveal a character's true thoughts to the audience. | How does dramatic irony create tension in a play you have studied? | Explain how cross-cutting and juxtaposition can be used to highlight a play's themes.

steps.title: Check your answers
steps.body: Three named devices (soliloquy, aside, direct address) with clear explanation of HOW they reveal truth and their different effects — soliloquy is extended, aside is brief and conspiratorial, direct ad | Specific example from a studied play where the audience knows more than a character — explain how this knowledge creates anticipation, fear or humour; link to the playwright's purpose. | Cross-cutting switches between scenes to show contrast; juxtaposition places opposing ideas together. Both highlight themes by forcing comparison. Give a specific example of each in practice.

steps.title: Exam tips
steps.body: Never confuse soliloquy (alone, extended) with aside (brief, others present) Always explain the EFFECT of the device on the audience Devices are CHOICES — always consider why the playwright used them Link devices to the play's overall themes and message
